1.topic: Borno under the Shehus: El-Kanemi, Shehu Umar and the fall of Borno
1.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. explain how Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi rose to power in Borno;
2. describe his achievements and those of Shehu Umar;
3. explain how the Sefawa dynasty ended in 1846;
4. describe the decline of the Shehus and the fall of Borno to Rabih and the British.

## Materials

Map of Borno, Lake Chad and the Fezzan; a chart of the Shehus; pictures of the Kukawa ruins and an old Kanuri horseman; extract from the El-Kanemi and Bello correspondence (short quotation).

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: can a scholar lead an army and rule a state? Recall the case of Usman dan Fodio and ask whether El-Kanemi was similar.

## Development

1. Background: the weakness of the Sefawa Mais in the early 19th century and the Fulani attack on Ngazargamu in 1808.
2. El-Kanemi: his origin (born at Murzuk in the Fezzan, with Kanembu connections), his scholarship, his defence of Borno with Kanembu and Shuwa Arab allies, his letters to Bello, his move to Kukawa (1814).
3. Rise to power: the Mai Dunama depended on him; he took power as Shehu while keeping the Mai as a figurehead.
4. Achievements: independence of Borno, a new capital, trade with Tripoli and Wadai, Islamic scholarship.
5. Shehu Umar (1837-1881): continued his father's work and ended the Mai dynasty in 1846.
6. Later Shehus and the fall: weakness, wars with Wadai, the arrival of Rabih in 1893, and British conquest in 1902.

## Class activity

Students make a timeline from 1808 to 1902 with six events.

## Evaluation

1. Why was Kukawa founded?
2. How did Rabih end the rule of the Shehus?

## Assignment

Problem set on the app, due Friday.

reading.title: From the Mais to the Shehus
reading.content:
# Borno under the Shehus

## The background

By 1800 Borno, ruled by the Sefawa dynasty, was weak. The Mais had lost control over the nobles, and the state was attacked by neighbours. In 1808, forces of the Fulani jihad captured the capital, Ngazargamu, and Mai Ahmad fled.

## The rise of El-Kanemi

Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi (about 1776-1837) was a Muslim scholar who was born in Murzuk in the Fezzan, but his family had come from Kanem. He came to Borno about 1806 and had great fame as a teacher. When the Fulani attacked, the Mai asked him for help. He gathered an army of Kanembu and Shuwa Arabs and drove the Fulani back, at Ngala in 1808. His reputation as a defender and a scholar grew, and Mai Dunama, who had been restored to the throne, became dependent on him.

El-Kanemi argued, in letters to Muhammad Bello, that Borno had been a Muslim state for centuries, so a jihad against it was not justified. In 1814 he founded a new capital, **Kukawa**, near Lake Chad, and he governed from it. He took the title **Shehu**, while the Mai remained as a figurehead without real power. He was the real ruler of Borno until his death in 1837.

## Achievements

1. He saved Borno from conquest and kept it independent of the Caliphate.
2. He built Kukawa as a centre of government, trade and learning.
3. He revived trade with Tripoli and Wadai across the Sahara, and drew revenue from it.
4. He supported Islamic scholars and justice.

## Shehu Umar (1837-1881)

El-Kanemi's son Umar took over as Shehu. In 1846 he overthrew and killed the last Mai, Ibrahim, ending the Sefawa dynasty, which had ruled for nearly a thousand years. He then ruled as the undisputed head. He kept order, supported trade and learning, and held off Wadai, but he lacked his father's ability, and his officials grew powerful.

## The decline and fall

Under the later Shehus, the court split into factions and the state was poor. In 1893 the warlord **Rabih az-Zubayr**, who had built an army in the east, conquered Borno, killed Shehu Hashim and ruled from Dikwa. The French defeated and killed Rabih in 1900, and the British took over most of Borno in 1902, restoring a Shehu as a ruler under British control.

2.topic: Christian missions in Nigeria: schools, hospitals and consequences
2.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. name the main missionary societies in Nigeria and where each worked;
2. describe their activities in education, health and the printing of books;
3. explain the contribution of missions to the training of Nigerians;
4. assess the positive and negative impact of missions, including the north-south educational gap.

## Materials

Map of Nigeria showing the mission centres (Badagry, Abeokuta, Lagos, Calabar, Onitsha, Zaria, Ibadan), pictures of the CMS Grammar School Lagos, Hope Waddell Training Institute and an old mission hospital, a chart of the missionary societies.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: which secondary school or hospital in your state was started by a church? List three, with the churches that founded them.

## Development

1. Societies and regions: CMS and Methodists in the south-west, the Church of Scotland and the Qua Iboe Mission in the south-east, Baptists in Ogbomoso and Ijaye, Catholics (SMA at Lagos 1868; Holy Ghost Fathers at Onitsha 1885), Sudan United Mission in the middle belt.
2. Education: primary schools, grammar schools, technical and teacher training; the Hope Waddell Training Institute (1895); the CMS Grammar School (1859).
3. Health, printing and agriculture: dispensaries and hospitals; Bible translations and newspapers; demonstration farms.
4. Impact: an educated class; nationalist leaders educated in mission schools; ending of twin killing and other practices; but also disrespect for traditional culture and unequal development between the north and the south because of the restrictions on missions in the emirates.

## Class activity

Students complete a chart listing five missions, the area each served and one contribution.

## Evaluation

1. Why did the colonial government keep missionaries out of the emirates?
2. Name two mission secondary schools.

## Assignment

Worksheet on the app, due Friday.

reading.content:
# Christian missionary activities in Nigeria

## The societies and their fields

After the first missionaries arrived at Badagry in 1842, many societies set up work in Nigeria:

- the **Methodists** and the **Church Missionary Society (CMS)** in the south-west, from Badagry to Abeokuta, Lagos and Ibadan;
- the **Southern Baptists**, at Ogbomoso and Ijaye;
- the **Church of Scotland** at Calabar (Hope Waddell, 1846) and the **Qua Iboe Mission** (Samuel Bill, 1887) in the south-east;
- the **Catholics**: the Society of African Missions at Lagos in 1868 and the Holy Ghost Fathers at Onitsha in 1885, led later by Bishop Joseph Shanahan, who built many schools in the east;
- the **Sudan United Mission** (founded in 1904 by Karl Kumm) in the middle belt and the north-east, while the CMS doctor Walter Miller began work at Zaria in 1900.

## Activities

**Education** was the main work. Missions built primary schools almost everywhere, and secondary schools such as the CMS Grammar School in Lagos (1859), the Methodist Boys' High School (1878), the Hope Waddell Training Institute at Calabar (1895) and St Gregory's College (1928). Some trained teachers and tradesmen. Until the 1950s, mission schools provided most of the schooling in Nigeria.

**Health.** Missions opened dispensaries and hospitals, such as the Wesley Guild Hospital at Ilesha and the hospital at Iyi-Enu, and trained nurses.

**Printing and language.** They translated the Bible into local languages, wrote the first books in Yoruba, Efik and Igbo and set up printing presses and newspapers.

**Agriculture and trades.** Some taught improved farming, carpentry and printing.

## Impact

**Positive.** Mission schools produced the first Nigerian teachers, clerks, doctors and clergy, and many nationalist leaders were mission-educated. Missions helped to end practices such as the killing of twins. They gave a base for Nigerian literacy and the study of local languages.

**Negative.** Converts were told to abandon traditional religion and customs, which caused divisions. The colonial government, to avoid trouble with Muslim rulers, kept missionaries out of most of the emirates. As a result the north fell far behind the south in western education, a gap that created regional inequality and affected national politics for decades. Competition among churches also led to quarrels and a wasteful duplication of schools.

3.topic: Yorubaland in the 19th century: Ibadan's rise and the coming of British control
3.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. describe the collapse of Oyo and its results for Yorubaland;
2. explain how Ibadan became the leading Yoruba power;
3. describe the main wars of the century: the Ijaye war and the Ekitiparapo (Kiriji) war;
4. explain how British pressure on Yorubaland increased from 1861 to 1893.

## Materials

Map of 19th-century Yorubaland showing Oyo, Ilorin, Ibadan, Abeokuta, Ijebu, Ijaye, Lagos and the Ekiti towns; pictures of the Kiriji war camp and of Bower's Tower in Ibadan; a timeline from 1829 to 1893.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: why is Ibadan so large today, when it was founded only about two hundred years ago? Collect guesses.

## Development

1. The fall of Oyo: Afonja, the Aare Ona Kakanfo of Oyo at Ilorin, and the Fulani scholar Alimi; the break-up of Oyo about 1835; the movement of peoples south.
2. The rise of Ibadan: founded about 1829 as a war camp; leaders such as Oluyole; a military state ruled by war leaders; the stopping of Ilorin's advance.
3. The rival centres: Abeokuta under Sodeke (from 1830), Ijaye under Kurunmi, Ijebu, and the Ekiti and Ijesa states.
4. The wars: the Ijaye war (1860-62), when Ibadan destroyed Ijaye; the Ekitiparapo war (1877-93).
5. British pressure: the annexation of Lagos (1861); Lagos Colony (1886); mediation in the wars; the Ijebu expedition of 1892; the Carter treaties of 1893.

## Class activity

Students draw a timeline of the century and mark the dates when Ibadan, Abeokuta and Lagos came to prominence.

## Evaluation

1. Who founded Abeokuta, and in what year?
2. Give one reason why the British wanted to end the Yoruba wars.

Worksheet on the app, due Friday.

reading.title: A century of war and change in Yorubaland
reading.content:
# Yorubaland in the 19th century

## The fall of Oyo

In the early 19th century the Oyo empire was weakened by quarrels among its leaders. Afonja, the military commander at Ilorin, rebelled against the Alaafin, and he invited the Fulani scholar Alimi to help him; Alimi's followers took over Ilorin, which became an emirate under Sokoto. About 1835 the Alaafin's capital, Oyo-Ile, was abandoned, and a new Oyo (Ago d'Oyo, later Oyo) was built further south. Refugees poured into the forest zone, and new towns grew.

## The rise of Ibadan

Ibadan began about 1829 as a war camp of soldiers from Oyo, Ife and Ijebu. The site was well placed, with fertile land and rocky hills for defence, in the area between the savanna and the forest. Soldiers of different origins competed for status, so Ibadan was ruled by **war leaders**, not by a king: the Bale, the Balogun and others, who were chosen by merit. Under such leaders as **Oluyole**, it checked the southward advance of Ilorin, gathered many refugees and farm slaves, and became the strongest Yoruba state.

## Rival centres and the wars

- **Abeokuta** was founded about 1830 by the Egba under **Sodeke** as a refuge among the rocks.
- **Ijaye** under **Kurunmi** was a strong town. In the **Ijaye war** (1860-62) Ibadan, supported by others, destroyed Ijaye.
- **Ijebu** closed its trade routes to outsiders.
- Ibadan's growing control of the Ekiti and Ijesa towns led the Ekiti, Ijesa, Ilorin and others to form the **Ekitiparapo**, an alliance. The **Ekitiparapo (Kiriji) war** lasted from 1877 to 1893, and the two sides were exhausted.

These wars hurt farming and trade, and many captives were sold.

## British pressure

The British were interested in ending the slave trade, protecting the palm oil trade and the safety of their missionaries and merchants. # Benin in the 19th century

## The kingdom and its trade

In the early 19th century Benin was still a powerful kingdom under an Oba with a large capital, Benin City, and a system of chiefs. Its Obas included **Osemwede** (1816-48) and **Adolo** (1848-88). The slave trade declined and the kingdom's wealth now came from **palm oil, palm kernels, rubber and ivory**. The Oba and his chiefs controlled the trade: foreign merchants had to deal with Benin traders at the coast, and the Oba taxed and sometimes restricted exports. The Itsekiri on the rivers acted as middlemen between Benin and the Europeans, which made some, like Nana Olomu, rich.

## British pressure

By the 1880s the British had organised the coast as the **Oil Rivers Protectorate**, and from 1893 the **Niger Coast Protectorate**. British traders complained that Benin's chiefs held back the trade, and that the Oba would not allow them free access to the interior. In 1892 Captain **Henry Gallwey**, the Vice-Consul, travelled to Benin and obtained a treaty from Oba **Ovonramwen** (who had come to the throne in 1888), by which Benin agreed to British protection and free trade. The Oba, however, did not mean to give up his control and the chiefs did not accept the treaty, so little changed.

## The crisis of 1897

In January 1897 the Acting Consul-General, **James Phillips**, decided to go to Benin with a party of officials, traders and carriers, to settle the trade question with the Oba. He ignored the Oba's request to wait until the **Igue festival**, a time of ritual when strangers were not welcome. The party was ambushed at **Ugbine** and nearly all of them were killed.

## The British expedition

The British sent a large punitive force under Admiral Harry Rawson. In February 1897 it captured and burned **Benin City**, and the Oba fled. He surrendered in August 1897 and was **exiled to Calabar**, where he died in 1914. Thousands of bronzes, ivory carvings and other treasures were taken to Britain and sold; many are now in museums abroad.

## Consequences

Benin lost its independence and was placed under British administration. Some chiefs who had resisted were tried and executed. The Oba's power was ended, and the kingdom's wealth and art were scattered. After Ovonramwen died in 1914, his son Eweka II was installed as Oba, but under British authority.

# The first phase of the British conquest, 1851-1900

## Lagos

Lagos was a busy port, and a centre of the slave trade even after Britain had made the trade illegal. In 1851 the ruler, Oba **Kosoko**, who had taken the throne by force from his uncle **Akitoye**, refused to give up the slave trade. Akitoye had fled and he asked the British Consul, John Beecroft, for help, promising to end the slave trade and to welcome missionaries and legitimate trade. In December 1851 the British navy **bombarded Lagos**. Kosoko fled and Akitoye was restored. A treaty banned the slave trade. In **1861**, after the Oba Docemo was pressed to cede it, Lagos was **annexed** as a British colony.

## The Niger and the Royal Niger Company

After the **Berlin Conference** (1884-85), Britain claimed the Niger. George **Goldie**'s National African Company made treaties with many chiefs and emirs, including Sokoto and Gwandu. In **1886** the company received a **royal charter** and became the Royal Niger Company, with the right to govern, tax and trade in the Niger area. It kept out rival traders by high duties. African middlemen lost their business, and in 1895 men of Nembe attacked the Company's depot at **Akassa**, because they said the Company had cut them off from their markets. The Company was crushed.

## The Oil Rivers and Niger Coast Protectorate

In **1885** the British declared the Oil Rivers Protectorate, run by consuls. It was renamed the **Niger Coast Protectorate** in 1893. Rulers who tried to control their own trade were removed:

- **Jaja of Opobo** built a rich state and sold palm oil direct to Liverpool, so British firms complained that he blocked them from the markets of the hinterland. In **1887** he was lured aboard a ship, tried and exiled to the West Indies, where he died in 1891.
- **Nana Olomu** of the Itsekiri, a wealthy trader, controlled the trade of the Benin River. His town at Ebrohimi was attacked by the navy in **1894**, and he was exiled.

## The position in 1900

In 1897 Benin fell, and in 1900 the Royal Niger Company's charter was ended. The government bought its rights and created the **Protectorate of Northern Nigeria**, under Frederick **Lugard**, and the **Protectorate of Southern Nigeria**. The conquest of the north, including Sokoto, would follow in 1903.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. describe how Britain completed the conquest of Nigeria between 1900 and 1903;
2. explain the reasons for the amalgamation of 1914 and its significance;
3. describe the central administration of colonial Nigeria;
4. explain indirect rule and why it succeeded in the north and failed in parts of the south-east;
5. describe the colonial economy and the social changes of the period.

Map of Nigeria showing the Northern and Southern Protectorates and the railway lines; pictures of Lugard, of a warrant chief and of the Lagos-Kano railway; a timeline of 1900 to 1960; a chart of exports.

1. The northern conquest: Lugard became High Commissioner in 1900, took Kano and Sokoto in 1903, and began indirect rule.
2. The south: the Aro expedition of 1901-02; the merging of Lagos Colony with the Southern Protectorate in 1906.
3. Amalgamation: 1 January 1914; Lugard as Governor-General; the reasons (financial, administrative, railway) and the significance (one country but a divided administration).
4. Central administration: the Governor, the Executive and Legislative Councils, Lieutenant-Governors, Residents, District Officers.
5. Indirect rule: how it worked in the emirates; how it was modified in the west; why it failed in the east (warrant chiefs and the Aba Women's War of 1929).

# Colonial Nigeria, 1900-1960

## Completing the conquest

In 1900 Frederick Lugard became High Commissioner of the **Protectorate of Northern Nigeria**. His force took Kano and Sokoto in 1903, and the last big battle was at Burmi in July 1903, where Sultan Attahiru I was killed. In the south, the **Aro expedition** of 1901-02 destroyed the power of the Aro. In 1906 the Colony of Lagos was joined to the Protectorate of Southern Nigeria.

## The amalgamation of 1914

On **1 January 1914** the Northern and Southern Protectorates were joined into the **Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria**, with Lugard as Governor-General (1914-19). The reasons were:

1. **Financial**: the north had a yearly deficit, while the south had a surplus from customs duties; joining them let the south pay for the north's needs.
2. **Administrative convenience**: one governor could run the railways, customs and postal service of the whole country.
3. **Railways**: the Lagos-Kano line, opened in 1912, linked the two regions.
4. Lugard's wish to spread **indirect rule** to the south and to unify the system.

The **significance** was that Nigeria became one country, but the north and the south remained separate in practice, with their own administrations, laws and education systems. This division later caused political problems.

## Central administration

At the top were the Governor, an Executive Council and, from 1914, a Nigerian Council, which could only advise. Below were Lieutenant-Governors, **Residents** in provinces and **District Officers**.

## Indirect rule

In the emirates, Lugard governed through the emirs, who kept their courts, collected taxes and obeyed British Residents. The system was cheap, and it worked because the emirates already had a well-organised government. In the west the Obas were used, though with less success. In the east there were no kings, so the British made **warrant chiefs** who were not respected. Their abuse and heavy tax led to the **Aba Women's War of 1929**.

## The colonial economy and social change

Nigeria produced cash crops (cocoa, groundnuts, palm products, cotton) and minerals (tin from Jos, coal from Enugu) for export, while it bought British manufactures. Railways and roads served the ports. Taxes were introduced. Schools, hospitals and newspapers spread, mainly in the south.

# The decolonisation of Nigeria, 1922-1960

## Origins of nationalism

Nationalism grew as educated Nigerians saw the injustice of colonial rule: the lack of a voice in government, heavy taxes, unequal pay, racial discrimination and the use of Nigerian goods for Britain's profit. Education, the press and the return of ex-servicemen from the wars made the demand stronger.

## The early period

The **Clifford Constitution of 1922** set up a Legislative Council and allowed the election of **four** Africans, three from Lagos and one from Calabar. It was the first time that Nigerians elected their representatives, so it led to the first political party, the **Nigerian National Democratic Party (NNDP)**, formed in 1923 by **Herbert Macaulay**. The constitution did not cover the north, and the vote was limited by property. In **1934** the Lagos Youth Movement, later the **Nigerian Youth Movement (NYM)**, was formed by young educated men such as Ernest Ikoli and H. O. Davies, and it was the first party to speak for the whole country.

## After the Second World War

In **1944** Macaulay and **Nnamdi Azikiwe** formed the **National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC)**. In 1946 Governor Richards introduced a new constitution, which created **regional assemblies** for the North, West and East, and which allowed the north into the legislative council, but did not give Nigerians a say in the executive. Other parties followed: the **Northern People's Congress (NPC)** in 1949, led by Ahmadu Bello and Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, and the **Action Group (AG)** in 1951, led by Obafemi Awolowo, which grew out of the cultural group Egbe Omo Oduduwa.

The **Macpherson Constitution of 1951** gave more power to the regions and to elected Nigerians. The **Lyttelton Constitution of 1954** made Nigeria a **federation** of three regions with a federal government. In 1957 the Eastern and Western Regions became self-governing, and the Northern Region followed in 1959. After conferences in London in 1957-58, Tafawa Balewa became the first Prime Minister, and in December 1959 federal elections were held. Nigeria became independent on **1 October 1960**.

## Objectives

1. describe the First Republic and the crises that ended it;
2. explain the coups of 1966 and the causes and results of the civil war;
3. describe the achievements of the Murtala/Obasanjo regime;

reading.content:
# Nigeria since independence, 1960-1984

## The First Republic (1960-66)

Nigeria began with a **parliamentary system** under Prime Minister **Abubakar Tafawa Balewa**, with **Nnamdi Azikiwe** as Governor-General (President from 1963, when Nigeria became a republic). There were three regions, and a fourth, the **Mid-West**, was created in 1963. Rivalry between the regions and parties led to serious crises: the **Western Region crisis** (1962), the quarrels over the **census** of 1962-63 and the disputed **federal election** of 1964, followed by violence in the West after the 1965 regional election.

## The coups and the civil war

On **15 January 1966** a group of army officers, led by Major Chukwuma Nzeogwu, overthrew the government and killed the Prime Minister, Balewa, and the premiers of the North and the West. General **Aguiyi-Ironsi** took over, but after he proposed a unitary system, northern officers staged a counter-coup in **July 1966**, in which he was killed, and **Yakubu Gowon** became head of state. There followed killings of many Igbo in the north. Talks at **Aburi**, Ghana, in January 1967 failed to hold. On 27 May 1967 Gowon created **twelve states**; on **30 May 1967** the Eastern Region leader, Lt-Col **Odumegwu Ojukwu**, declared the **Republic of Biafra**. The **civil war** began in July 1967 and ended in January 1970 with the surrender of Biafra. Gowon declared 'no victor, no vanquished', and began the three Rs: **reconciliation, rehabilitation and reconstruction**.

## Murtala Muhammed and Obasanjo (1975-79)

In July 1975 General **Murtala Muhammed** took over from Gowon. He was assassinated in February 1976 in an attempted coup and was succeeded by General **Olusegun Obasanjo**. The regime created **nineteen states** (1976), began **Universal Primary Education** (1976), chose **Abuja** as the new federal capital, reformed local government, set up a Constitution Drafting Committee, and issued the Land Use Decree (1978). It handed over to a civilian government on **1 October 1979**.

## The Second Republic (1979-83)

The 1979 constitution set up a **presidential system** on the American model. **Shehu Shagari** of the National Party of Nigeria (NPN) became President. The government was weakened by falling oil prices, heavy borrowing, corruption, and disputes over the 1983 elections, and it was overthrown on 31 December 1983.

## The Buhari/Idiagbon regime (1983-85)

Major-General **Muhammadu Buhari** and Brigadier **Tunde Idiagbon** launched the **War Against Indiscipline** (WAI), tried officials for corruption and cut imports, but banned criticism and detained journalists. They were overthrown in August 1985.

reading.content:
# Nigeria, 1985-2000

## The Babangida regime (1985-93)

General **Ibrahim Babangida** took power in August 1985. In 1986 he introduced the **Structural Adjustment Programme (SAP)**: devaluation of the naira, removal of subsidies, support for local production and a reduction of imports. SAP was meant to repair the economy, but its effects were heavy on ordinary people: the cost of living rose and wages fell.

He promised a return to civil rule. His programme was long and was often changed. The government set up a Political Bureau, created agencies such as MAMSER (for mass mobilisation) and formed **two parties by decree**: the **Social Democratic Party (SDP)** and the **National Republican Convention (NRC)**. Politicians were banned and unbanned, party primaries were cancelled, and the handover date was moved several times, from 1990 to 1992 and then to 1993.

## The June 12, 1993 election

The presidential election of **12 June 1993** was seen as one of the freest in Nigeria's history. Observers' results showed that **M. K. O. Abiola** of the SDP had won. Before the results were all declared, the government **annulled** the election. There were strikes and riots, especially in the south-west, and Babangida **stepped aside** in August 1993.

## The Interim National Government and Abacha

Babangida handed power to an **Interim National Government (ING)** headed by **Ernest Shonekan**. It was declared illegal by a court and lasted less than three months. On **17 November 1993** General **Sani Abacha** removed it and took power.

## The Abacha regime (1993-98)

Abacha dissolved the political structures, jailed opponents and arrested Abiola in 1994 after he declared himself President. In 1995 the writer **Ken Saro-Wiwa** and eight Ogoni activists were hanged, which led to Nigeria's suspension from the Commonwealth. Abacha planned his own transition, but he died on 8 June 1998, and Abiola died in July.

## The return to civil rule

General **Abdulsalami Abubakar** organised a short transition. Elections were held in early 1999, and **Olusegun Obasanjo** was sworn in as President on **29 May 1999**, beginning the **Fourth Republic**.

## Emerging issues

By 2000, Nigeria faced **poverty**, **corruption**, **youth unemployment**, **religious and ethnic violence** (in Kaduna, Kano and Jos) and armed unrest in the Niger Delta.
